newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA DOUBTS FRENCH EX-DEFENCE MINISTER SPY CASE.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA DOUBTS FRENCH EX-DEFENCE MINISTER SPY CASE.

text.p: Bulgarian ex-spook doubts whether Bulgarian secret services told France four years ago that the late Socialist ex-defence minister Charles Hernu had been a communist agent early in his career, Bulgarian television said.

"This is not very likely because in this profession friendship and money do not mix," Todor Boyadjiev, head of the Bulgarian Euro-Atlantic Intelligence Forum (BUAIF), said in an interview with state television on Wednesday.
BUAIF is a local think-tank grouping former intelligence officers who were forced to resign after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

"However after the reorganisation of these (intelligence) services, there were cases of literal treason, when state secrets were sold for pennies," said Boyadjiev, who was a senior Interior Ministry official until 1992.
Jacques Fournet, former chief of DST counter-intelligence, told France 3 television he could not check the report, but passed it on to then president Francois Mitterrand.
He said Mitterrand decided to classify the report as state secret, since Hernu who served as defence minister in 1981-85, had died in 1990 and could not defend himself from the charges.
"DST was not able to verify what was in this report...We can regard this file as somewhat suspicious," Fournet said.
The weekly L'Express earlier quoted secret files as showing that Hernu, a friend of Mitterrand's, had spied for the Soviet Union and other communist countries in the 1950s and 1960s.
"It is also very likely that here we have a case of sheer sensationalism," said Boydjiev.
Biographer Jean Guisnel said Hernu was too junior to know anything worthwhile at the time. The files did not say if he kept working for the east after he became defence minister.

L'Express said Hernu was recruited as a rising political star by a Bulgarian spy in Paris in 1953, and was paid by Bulgaria, Romania and the Soviet Union for at least a decade for supplying reports about French politics.

The Bulgarian diplomat Raiko Nikolov, who allegedly recruited Hernu, told Bulgarian state television in a telephone interview that "he indeed knew Mr. Hernu, but only in the way in which a diplomat has social ties with many people."
L'Express compared the Hernu case to the espionage scandals of British spy Kim Philby and Germany's Gunther Guillaume.
"I'm stunned, I knew nothing about this, like all the French people," Hernu's cabinet colleague Jacques Delors, finance minister from 1981 to 1984, told Europe-1 radio.

The Socialist Party, in which Hernu was a key figure, cast doubt on the report and said all that mattered was whether Hernu had been "an intransigent protagonist for national independence, European and French security; the answer is yes."
Former spy barons also urged authorities to shed light on what if anything Hernu allegedly supplied his communist patrons.

"I've no idea whether this is true or false. Hernu was anti-Soviet and anti-communist, but on questions (of spying) there is a complete break between public and private life," Pierre Marion, former head of the DGSE secret service, which answers to the Defence Ministry, told Reuters.
"These accusations are too serious not to be cleared up."
Patrice Hernu, one of the late minister's sons, branded the report "a fabrication coarsely sown together" and urged President Jacques Chirac to shed light on the affair.
L'Express quoted the files as saying Hernu was known by the codenames "Andre" or "Dinu", and had been paid monthly for his work, which included portraits of politicians like Mitterrand.
It said he accepted the equivalent of 300,000 francs ($60,000) in 1958 to fund an election campaign to parliament, but lost despite the cash.

Hernu resigned in disgrace from the defence ministry in 1985 after French agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland, New Zealand, as the vessel was preparing to protest against French nuclear testing in the South Pacific.
